content: The benefits of implementing these guidelines in lowand middle-income countries were outlined. However, no efforts were made to systematically gather the values and preferences of the individuals targeted by these guidelines. Data derived from observational studies were considered to carry a risk of bias. If the risk of bias due to methodological issues, imprecision, inconsistency, or lack of directness was not deemed very serious, the quality of evidence was rated as moderate. Consequently, the highest possible quality of evidence from observational studies was classified as moderate. The recommendations were developed and drafted following the procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (WHO, 2012) and were guided by the quality of evidence using the GRADE methodology. A Steering Group, composed of members from various relevant WHO departments, oversaw the guideline review process. A Guideline Development Group (GDG) was established to define scoping questions, review evidence and complementary assessments, reach consensus, and update or establish new recommendations. The GDG included a balanced mix of scientists, researchers, program managers, healthcare providers, and implementing partners, ensuring gender and geographic representation. The specific roles and affiliations of GDG members are acknowledged in the document. A Peer Review Group was also formed to review the recommendations developed by the GDG. The Steering Group defined the scope of the recommendations based on program experience and a review of existing guidelines. Major Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) questions were formulated and are listed under each condition in the recommendations section. All GDG members were required to sign and submit a Declaration of Interests before participating in meetings. WHO staff assessed these declarations to identify potential conflicts of interest that could limit participation. After discussion and consideration of expertise, participation was allowed where appropriate. The Steering Group supervised the systematic reviews and GRADE tables for the PICO questions. The PICO questions were reviewed and approved by the Steering Group and the Guidelines Review Committee (GRC). Evidence retrieval followed the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Protocols for systematic reviews included search terms, strategies, and criteria for inclusion and exclusion. Medline and Embase databases were used to identify peer-reviewed publications, and ongoing studies were searched on clinical trial registries. Each step was discussed with the GDG through teleconferences or meetings. The quality of evidence for treatment interventions was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low based on GRADE definitions. The GDG reviewed systematic reviews and GRADE tables to identify missing evidence, provide comments, and suggest revisions. Decision-making tables were drafted to include benefits and risks of interventions, cost and feasibility of implementation, and acceptability to program managers, policymakers, healthcare providers, and people living with HIV. The final consensus meeting of the GDG was held in Geneva in September 2013. Evidence summaries, GRADE reviews, and risk-benefit analyses were reviewed, and final recommendations were approved. Decisions were made by consensus, with opposing views resolved through discussion or voting when necessary. Draft guidelines were circulated to the GDG and Peer Review Group for comments, which were incorporated as appropriate. An advisory group on Kaposi sarcoma participated in teleconferences and provided input on drafts. The GDG identified knowledge gaps requiring primary research, prioritizing those that were feasible, innovative, and likely to improve management of the conditions addressed in the guidelines. Recommendations based on low or very low-quality evidence require further research, while those based on moderate or high-quality evidence do not. The guidelines will be regularly updated as new evidence becomes available, with major reviews every five years. The next major update is planned for 2019 under the oversight of the WHO GRC. Simultaneously, a multi-agency group led by WHO has been developing a diagnostic tool for HIV/AIDS-related skin conditions. This tool complements the treatment-focused guidelines by aiding diagnosis. It was developed through expert input and field-tested in clinics in Tanzania, South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya. The tool includes a topography map, decision-making tree, and picture atlas, with 90% agreement between field practitioners and dermatologists in a pilot study. Future iterations will include globally relevant skin diseases and conditions that indicate the need for HIV testing or biopsy. Guiding principles for HIV testing, ART initiation, and general care emphasize offering immediate HIV testing to individuals with unknown status presenting with relevant conditions and evaluating known HIV-positive individuals for ART eligibility. These principles align with WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV care and antiretroviral use. Provider-initiated testing and counseling are recommended in all health facilities in generalized epidemics and for specific populations in concentrated or low-level epidemics. Early ART initiation improves survival and reduces community-level HIV incidence. Current WHO guidance recommends ART for all individuals with HIV and a CD4 count of ≤500 cells/mm³, prioritizing those with advanced disease or CD4 ≤350 cells/mm³. ART initiation is also recommended for individuals with active TB, severe hepatitis B, pregnant or breastfeeding women, children under five, and those in serodiscordant relationships. Simplified, less toxic, and more convenient fixed-dose combination regimens are preferred for first-line ART, ideally as once-daily regimens for adults, adolescents, and children over three years. For children under three, this may not yet be feasible. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for long-term use in individuals with conditions mentioned in the guidelines. Personal hygiene is emphasized as a preventive and care measure, particularly for infants. Referral to higher-level facilities should be considered if conditions do not respond to recommended treatment.
